result:
You gave me 1000 words. No topic, no prompt, no direction. Just space.

So here is what comes to me:

---

I think about my grandmother's kitchen drawer.

Not the whole kitchen - just the drawer. The junk drawer everyone has. Hers had the usual: dead batteries, rubber bands, takeout menus for restaurants that closed in 2008, a tape measure, birthday candles. But she also had this habit of saving bread ties. Those little plastic squares. She had hundreds of them in a jam jar.

I once asked her why.

"They're good for something," she said. "Just haven't figured out what yet."

I think about that jar a lot. How we all have jars of bread ties. Things we keep because throwing them away feels more wrong than keeping them.

You gave me 1000 words and my first instinct is to not waste them. To make something Worthy of 1000 words. A proper story with an arc and a moral. But maybe the most honest thing is to just think out loud and see what sticks.

So here it is. A few things I can't stop thinking about lately:

**1. The weight of early mornings.**

There is a specific kind of morning that only exists between 5 and 6 a.m. The world hasn't decided to be awake yet. The light is blue and undecided. If you go outside then, even in a city, you can hear birds you forget live there. I used to hate waking up early. Now I collect those mornings like other people collect vinyl. On Sunday I woke up at 5:17 for no reason, made coffee, and sat on my kitchen floor and watched the sun hit the fridge. Nothing happened. It was perfect.

We talk about big moments, but I think we are mostly made of those quiet, unlogged hours. The ones that will never make it into a photo album. Waiting for toast to pop. Finding a good parking spot. The way your dog sighs when he finally gets comfortable.

**2. That we are all living in the middle.**

We love stories because they have beginnings and endings. But no one has ever lived at the beginning or the end. We are always in the middle of something. Middle of becoming a person, middle of healing from something, middle of missing someone, middle of a Tuesday. 

I had a friend who used to say "I'll be happy when..." I'll be happy when I get the promotion, when I move, when I pay this off. He was always living in the preview. I think I do it too. But lately I've been trying to notice the middle. To say, "This is it. This middle part where nothing is resolved? This is the whole thing."

It's terrifying and also a relief.

**3. A short story, because I have the words:**

Mara inherited a lighthouse that didn't need to be a lighthouse anymore. The coast had shifted, the GPS had made it obsolete. When she got the keys, the realtor said, "It's mostly symbolic now."

She went anyway. 112 iron steps in a spiral. The lens at the top was still there, huge and dusty, like a sleeping eye.

She didn't know how to be a lighthouse keeper, so she just lived there. She brought up a kettle and a bookshelf, one book at a time. She learned that the wind has different voices depending on which window it hits.

One night a storm came that knocked out power for the whole town below. Her light was the only one they had left, even though ships didn't need it. She cleaned the lens for three hours, lit the old lamp with oil she found in a shed, and it worked. A soft, sweeping gold over the black water.

Nothing was saved that night. No dramatic rescue. But in the morning, a fisherman came up the hill with a thermos and said, "We could see you from town. We knew where we were."

That's what I want, I think. Not to save anyone. Just to be a steady light that says *we knew where we were.*

**4. The last thing.**

If you gave me 1000 words, I have used about 600. That means I have 400 left to waste or save. And I think I'll save them. On purpose.

Because not everything needs to be filled to the edge. My grandmother never did find a use for all those bread ties. But when she died and we emptied the drawer, my mother and I laughed for ten minutes straight looking at that jar. Hundreds of tiny, useless, colorful squares. It was so *her* - saving things just in case they might matter.

So I'll leave these last words empty. Not because I have nothing to say, but because you don't always have to use all of what you're given to make it count.

Keep the rest in your pocket. For the next quiet morning, or the middle you're in, or whenever you need a small light.

I'm glad you were here for these words.
